gotchas: InternalError is NOT a GraphQL error. mkResponse(result: Result[Json]) calls M.raiseError(err) for InternalError, so it propagates as an effect-level failure (e.g. an IO error) rather than appearing in the errors array. Use Result.failure / Problem for client-facing errors and Result.internalError only for genuine bugs/unexpected conditions.

Failure has no value, Warning does. The whole point of Warning is to keep partial data while still reporting problems — it serialises to a response with BOTH data and errors. Choosing failure vs warning during elaboration changes whether the client gets any data (see the explicit comment in QueryDirectivesSuite: 'We could make this fail the whole query by yielding Elab.failure here').

Problem equality ignores extensions. eqProblem is Eq.by(p => (p.message, p.locations, p.path)) — two Problems with different extensions compare equal. Tests relying on extensions must compare the encoded JSON (asJson), not the Problem values.

Empty locations/path/extensions vanish from the JSON. The ProblemEncoder omits any empty field, so Problem("foo") encodes to just {"message":"foo"}. Don't assert on the presence of those keys when they're empty.

mkResponse(data=None, errors=empty) injects a synthetic error. If both data is absent and the error chain is empty it emits {"errors":[{"message":"Invalid query"}]} — an empty Result should never reach this path in normal flow, but a custom interpreter that returns no data and no problems will get this catch-all message.

combine / Semigroup downgrades Failure to Warning when the other side has a value. Result.combine of a Failure with a Success yields a Warning (problems + the success value), not a Failure. This is intentional Ior-like accumulation but can surprise callers expecting failure to dominate. InternalError, however, always dominates / short-circuits.

flatMap problem-merge order matters. In flatMap of a Warning whose continuation is a Warning, problems are concatenated as `problems ++ fps` (outer first). When relying on ordered error reporting, be aware combinators preserve a specific accumulation order (and Applicative ap orders them ff-then-fa).

Parallel/Applicative accumulate; Monad short-circuits. parMapN (via grackleParallelForResult) and the Applicative ap collect problems from all operands, but flatMap/for-comprehensions short-circuit on the first Failure/InternalError. Use parMapN / mapN / traverse when you want all errors reported at once (this is how the compiler reports multiple validation errors).

ValidationFailure is a different axis from Problem. ValidationFailure (with Severity Error/Warning/Info, ANSI colouring, ValidationException) is used at Schema/Mapping construction & validation time, not for per-request GraphQL errors. Don't confuse Result.Warning (runtime, a Problem) with Severity.Warning (a validation diagnostic).

fromOption/fromEither have DummyImplicit-disambiguated String overloads. The Problem and String variants of fromOption/fromEither (and Option#toResult) are distinguished by an implicit DummyImplicit because they'd otherwise erase to the same signature — passing the wrong by-name type can pick the unexpected overload.

Result.warning(String, value) wraps the string in a Problem with no path/locations. Warnings/failures created from bare strings have empty locations and path; positional info must be attached explicitly (e.g. via Problem(msg, locations, path)) or earlier in the pipeline, otherwise the errors array entry is message-only.

summary: The Generic backend (module `grackle-generic`, package `grackle.generic`) lets you serve a GraphQL schema directly from ordinary Scala ADTs (case classes and sealed traits) without writing per-field mappings. Its core abstraction is the typeclass `CursorBuilder[T]`, which knows how to build a Grackle `Cursor` over a value of type `T`; instances for primitives, `Option`, `List`, Scala `Enumeration` values and any Circe-`Encoder` leaf are provided implicitly, and instances for product types (objects) and coproduct types (interfaces/unions) are derived semi-automatically via `semiauto.deriveObjectCursorBuilder` / `deriveInterfaceCursorBuilder` (shapeless on Scala 2, shapeless3 on Scala 3). A `GenericMapping[F]` wires these builders into the rest of Grackle by exposing `GenericField(fieldName, value)` field mappings and a `genericCursor` helper. There is no `@GraphQLField` or any other annotation in this codebase — derivation is purely structural (case-class field names must match GraphQL field names, and customisation is done explicitly with `renameField`/`transformFieldNames`/`transformField`).

keyConcepts.name: CursorBuilder[T] typeclass
keyConcepts.explanation: The central abstraction (modules/generic/src/main/scala/CursorBuilder.scala). A CursorBuilder[T] carries the GraphQL `tpe: Type` it produces and a `build(context, focus, parent, env): Result[Cursor]` method. Everything in the generic backend is about obtaining a CursorBuilder for your domain types. Summon one with `CursorBuilder[T]` (the apply on the companion).

keyConcepts.name: Implicit leaf/collection builders
keyConcepts.explanation: CursorBuilder.scala provides implicit instances for String, Int, Long, Float, Double, Boolean (PrimitiveCursor-backed leaves), `Option[T]` (nullable), `List[T]` (list), Scala `Enumeration#Value` (serialised via toString), and a fallback `leafCursorBuilder[T]` for any type with a Circe `Encoder[T]`. These are resolved automatically when deriving products/coproducts, so each field type must have a CursorBuilder in scope.

keyConcepts.name: Semiauto product derivation (objects)
keyConcepts.explanation: `semiauto.deriveObjectCursorBuilder[T](tpe)` derives an ObjectCursorBuilder[T] for a case class, mapping each case-class field name to a sub-CursorBuilder resolved for that field's type. The GraphQL object type is supplied explicitly as `tpe` (a schema.ref). Field names are matched structurally to the case-class member names.

keyConcepts.name: Semiauto coproduct derivation (interfaces/unions)
keyConcepts.explanation: `semiauto.deriveInterfaceCursorBuilder[T](tpe)` derives a CursorBuilder[T] for a sealed trait / sealed ADT whose subtypes each already have a CursorBuilder. At runtime it selects the concrete branch, builds with that branch's builder, and wraps it so the cursor reports the interface type but can `narrow` to the concrete subtype. Used for GraphQL `interface` (and union) types.

keyConcepts.name: GenericField mapping
keyConcepts.explanation: `GenericField(fieldName, value)` (defined in GenericMappingLike) is a FieldMapping that attaches a Scala value plus its implicit CursorBuilder to a schema field — typically used on the root Query ObjectMapping to expose the in-memory data. `subtree` is true and it can be `hidden`. GenericMapping overrides `mkCursorForMappedField` to dispatch GenericField to its builder.

keyConcepts.name: Field customisation combinators
keyConcepts.explanation: ObjectCursorBuilder[T] adds `renameField(from, to)`, `transformFieldNames(f)`, and `transformField[U](name)(f: T => Result[U])`. transformField is the key escape hatch: it replaces a derived field with a computed/effect-free resolution (e.g. resolving foreign-key id lists to nested objects), which is also how recursion between types is broken.

keyConcepts.name: Recursion via lazy/by-name builders
keyConcepts.explanation: CursorBuilder implicit parameters are taken by-name (`implicit cb: => CursorBuilder[T]`), GenericField stores a `() => CursorBuilder[T]` thunk, and Impl's fieldMap is a lazy `=> FieldMap[T]`. This laziness lets mutually-recursive types (Programme <-> Production) and self-referential graphs define their builders as implicit vals without initialization-order deadlock.

keyConcepts.name: genericCursor / DeferredCursor
keyConcepts.explanation: `genericCursor(path, env, t)` builds a Cursor for a value at an arbitrary path: at the root it builds eagerly; otherwise it returns a `DeferredCursor` that defers building until the surrounding context/parent is known. This is what you return from a RootEffect.computeCursor to plug a generic value into the effectful root.

gotchas: There is NO @GraphQLField (or any) annotation in the generic backend — derivation is purely structural. The case-class field NAME must exactly match the GraphQL field name; to differ, use renameField/transformFieldNames. The FOCUS hint about @GraphQLField does not apply to this codebase.

The GraphQL Type is always passed explicitly to deriveObjectCursorBuilder[T](tpe) / deriveInterfaceCursorBuilder[T](tpe) / deriveLeafCursorBuilder[T](tpe). Nothing is inferred from the Scala type name; a mismatch between case-class fields and the schema type's fields is only caught at query time (e.g. 'No field ...').

Implicit method names are misspelled: optionCursorBuiler and listCursorBuiler (missing the 'd'). If you ever reference them by name (rather than relying on implicit resolution) you must use the typo'd spelling.
Long maps to IntType and Double/Float both map to FloatType in the primitive builders (CursorBuilder.scala). There is no separate GraphQL type for Long/Double — they share Int/Float.

leafCursorBuilder is an implicit fallback for ANY type with a Circe Encoder and it reports StringType. This means a domain type with an Encoder in scope will silently be treated as a String leaf even where you intended an object — and it can shadow/compete with object derivation. Custom scalars rely on this (java.time, UUID, Genre).

CursorBuilder implicits are by-name (=> CursorBuilder[T]) and GenericField captures a () => CursorBuilder[T] thunk; Impl.fieldMap is lazy. This is deliberate for recursion. If you eagerly force a builder during construction of a mutually-recursive pair you can reintroduce initialization-order problems.

Recursion between object types is NOT automatic from the ADT shape — RecursionSuite models references as id Strings and resolves them with transformField. A naive directly-recursive case class (holding the related object) would require the related type's CursorBuilder to exist, which the by-name machinery allows, but the test/demo pattern is id-plus-resolver.

transformField's replacement type U must have its own CursorBuilder in scope (the implicit cb: => CursorBuilder[U] parameter). For resolveFriends returning Result[Option[List[Character]]] this means CursorBuilder[Option[List[Character]]] (via the Option/List/interface builders) must resolve.

The interface/union cursor wraps the concrete branch's cursor; narrow only succeeds when subtpe <:< interfaceTpe AND concreteTpe <:< subtpe (CursorImpl.narrowsTo). Querying a subtype-only field without a matching fragment, or narrowing to an unrelated type, yields an internalError 'cannot be narrowed'.

Scala 2 vs Scala 3 use different derivation engines (shapeless vs shapeless3) in separate source roots (scala-2/genericmapping2.scala, scala-3/genericmapping3.scala) but expose the identical public surface (MkObjectCursorBuilder/MkInterfaceCursorBuilder/ObjectCursorBuilder). Don't document shapeless-specific implicits (Generic.Aux, K0.ProductInstances) as public API — they are derivation internals.

GenericMapping requires an implicit MonadThrow[F]; the in-memory examples use IO. Fields resolved purely from data don't run effects, but RootEffect.computeCursor + genericCursor is the path for effectful roots.

summary: The Circe backend lets you build a Grackle `Mapping` whose data source is in-memory circe `Json` rather than a database. The whole subsystem lives in a single source file, `modules/circe/src/main/scala/circemapping.scala`, and exposes two entry points: the abstract class `CirceMapping[F]` (extend this for a standalone JSON-backed mapping) and the trait `CirceMappingLike[F]` (mix this into other mappings — notably `SqlMappingLike` extends it — to splice JSON-valued fields into a non-JSON mapping). Field-level building blocks are `CirceField` (a constant `Json` subtree) and `CursorFieldJson` (a `Json` subtree computed from the parent `Cursor`); both produce a `CirceCursor`, the `Cursor` implementation that walks a `Json` value against the GraphQL schema. The backend is the canonical choice for fixtures/tests, statically-known data, REST/HTTP responses already in JSON, and effectful roots that yield JSON, via the `RootEffect.computeJson`/`computeEncodable` and `RootStream.computeJson`/`computeEncodable` syntax extensions. It requires no database; `F` only needs a `cats.MonadThrow`.

keyConcepts.name: CirceMapping vs CirceMappingLike
keyConcepts.explanation: `CirceMappingLike[F]` is the trait carrying all behavior (cursor construction, field mappings, root-effect syntax). `CirceMapping[F]` is just `abstract class CirceMapping[F](implicit M: MonadThrow[F]) extends Mapping[F] with CirceMappingLike[F]` — the convenient base class for a standalone JSON-backed mapping. Use the trait when you want to add JSON fields to an existing mapping (e.g. a SQL mapping) rather than start from scratch; `SqlMappingLike` already does `extends CirceMappingLike[F]`, which is why `CirceField`/`CursorFieldJson` are usable in SQL mappings.

keyConcepts.name: CirceCursor walks Json against the schema
keyConcepts.explanation: `CirceCursor` is a `Cursor` that holds a `Json` focus plus the GraphQL `Context` (current type). Navigation methods (`field`, `asList`, `narrow`, `asNullable`, `asLeaf`) interpret the JSON shape through the lens of the GraphQL type at that point. Object fields are looked up by name in the JSON object; lists require a JSON array; leaves are validated against the expected scalar/enum type.

keyConcepts.name: CirceField — constant JSON subtree
keyConcepts.explanation: `CirceField(fieldName, value: Json)` maps a GraphQL field to a fixed `Json` value. The entire subtree under that field is served from this JSON. Its `subtree` flag is true, meaning Grackle treats it as opaque: the JSON inside is matched structurally against the schema and the rest of the typeMappings are NOT consulted for fields inside it (see CircePrioritySuite).

keyConcepts.name: CursorFieldJson — computed JSON subtree
keyConcepts.explanation: `CursorFieldJson(fieldName, f: Cursor => Result[Json], required: List[String], hidden)` is like `CirceField` but the JSON is computed from the parent `Cursor` (so it can read sibling fields named in `required`). This is the bridge used to splice JSON into non-JSON backends, e.g. decoding a DB column into a JSON object in SqlCursorJsonMapping.

keyConcepts.name: Opaque-subtree priority semantics
keyConcepts.explanation: Because `CirceFieldMapping.subtree == true`, a JSON value supplied by `CirceField`/`CursorFieldJson` is self-contained. `CirceCursor.field` first looks for the field inside the current JSON object and only falls back to `mkCursorForField` (the mapping's other typeMappings) when the JSON object does not contain that field. CircePrioritySuite demonstrates this: `present` has `name` in its JSON so the literal 'Bob' wins; `fallback` omits it so the explicit `CirceField('name', 'Steve')` mapping on `Monkey` is used.

keyConcepts.name: Effectful JSON roots
keyConcepts.explanation: `CirceMappingLike` enriches `RootEffect` and `RootStream` companion objects with `computeJson` (effect yields `Json`) and `computeEncodable[A]` (effect yields `A` with a circe `Encoder[A]`). Both ultimately call core `computeCursor`, wrapping the result in a `CirceCursor` via `circeCursor(path, env, json)`. `computeCursor` can also be used directly with `circeCursor(...)` for full control (CirceEffectData shows all three).

keyConcepts.name: circeCursor helper and root vs nested
keyConcepts.explanation: `circeCursor(path, env, value)` builds the right cursor for a position: if `path.isRoot` it makes a `CirceCursor` at `Context(path.rootTpe)`; otherwise it returns a `DeferredCursor` that builds the `CirceCursor` once the parent context is known. In effect handlers you choose `Path.from(p.rootTpe)` (rooted: JSON includes the field name) vs `p` (nested: JSON is the field's value) — CirceEffectData contrasts `qux` (rooted) with `foo` (nested).

gotchas: CirceField/CursorFieldJson are opaque subtrees (`subtree == true`). `CirceCursor.field` looks inside the JSON object first and only falls back to other typeMappings when the JSON lacks the field. So an explicit field mapping for a nested type is shadowed whenever the JSON already provides that field (see CircePrioritySuite: 'present' returns 'Bob', not 'Steve').

Custom GraphQL scalars served from JSON still need a `LeafMapping[T]` (e.g. `LeafMapping[BigDecimal](BigDecimalType)`), otherwise `asLeaf`'s catch-all `case _: ScalarType if !focus.isObject => focus.success` will pass the raw JSON through but the type won't be registered/encoded as you expect. Built-in scalars (Int/Float/String/Boolean/ID) need no mapping.

`asLeaf` for `IntType` re-parses through `_.toLong` and emits `Json.fromLong`; a JSON number that is not integral (or overflows Long) fails with 'Expected Int found ...'. `FloatType` passes the number through unchanged. Enums must be JSON strings whose value is a declared enum value, else an internalError.

JSON fields not present in the GraphQL schema are simply unreachable by queries — querying them yields 'No field X for type ...' (CirceSuite 'hidden' test). But such extra JSON fields CAN be read internally by a `CursorField`/`CursorFieldJson` via `required` + `c.fieldAs[Json](name)` (CirceData computeField reads 'hidden').

`narrowsTo` (interface/union fragment matching) inspects the JSON object's keys: a subtype matches only if every non-nullable field of the subtype is present in the JSON object AND every JSON key corresponds to a field of the subtype. Missing required keys or extra unknown keys cause the narrow to fail. This drives `__typename` resolution for interfaces (CirceSuite 'introspection'/'fragments').

In effect handlers, choosing the path matters: `circeCursor(p, e, json)` (or `RootEffect.computeJson` which uses `p`) expects `json` to be the *value of the field*; `circeCursor(Path.from(p.rootTpe), e, json)` expects `json` to be an object *containing the field name*. Mixing these up yields a shape mismatch. CirceEffectData contrasts 'qux' (rooted, wraps in { "qux": {...} }) with 'foo' (nested, just {...}).

`CirceCursor.mkChild` resets the child's `Env` to `Env.empty` (the new cursor does not inherit the parent's env). `withEnv` on a CirceCursor adds to the existing env. Don't rely on env propagating downward through navigation automatically.

`CirceMapping` requires only `MonadThrow[F]`, but the effectful root syntax examples and tests use `Sync[F]`/`IO` because they perform real effects (e.g. SignallingRef). The base class itself imposes no Sync requirement.

`CirceMappingLike` is the trait you mix into non-circe backends; `SqlMappingLike extends CirceMappingLike`, which is the only reason `CirceField`/`CursorFieldJson`/`circeCursor` are available inside SQL mappings (SqlCursorJsonMapping uses CursorFieldJson to decode a DB column into JSON).

subsystem: SQL mappings (joins, embedding, interfaces, unions, jsonb)
summary: Grackle's SQL mappings let you serve a GraphQL schema directly from relational tables by declaring, per GraphQL object type, how each field maps to a SQL column (`SqlField`), a sub-object reached by a join (`SqlObject` + `Join`), or a `jsonb` column whose JSON sub-tree is navigated in-process (`SqlJson`). The mapping machinery lives in `modules/sql-core/src/main/scala/SqlMapping.scala` under the `SqlMappingLike[F]` trait, which is database-agnostic; backend modules (`doobie-core`, `skunk`) supply concrete `Codec`/`Encoder`/`Fragment` types and a `col` helper. Grackle compiles a GraphQL query into a single (or few) SQL statement(s), joining and embedding rows as needed, and handles interfaces/unions by mapping all subtypes onto shared columns and using an `SqlDiscriminator` to pick the concrete type per row. Key column references are `ColumnRef` (built via `col`) grouped under `TableDef`/`RootDef`; joins are `Join` of one-or-more `(ColumnRef, ColumnRef)` condition pairs, enabling composite-key and multi-table chained joins. Embedded (synopses-style) objects share a parent table and are addressed with `PrefixedMapping` when the same GraphQL type appears under different parents.

keyConcepts.name: ColumnRef and the col helper
keyConcepts.explanation: Every mapped column is a `ColumnRef(table, column, codec, scalaTypeName, pos)`. You never construct it directly; you call `col(name, codec)` inside a `TableDef`/`RootDef`, which captures the table name (via an implicit `TableName`), the Scala type name, and source position. Two `ColumnRef`s are equal iff their table and column names match (codec is ignored in equals/hashCode), so the same physical column referenced twice is treated as one.

keyConcepts.name: TableDef / RootDef / TableName
keyConcepts.explanation: `class TableDef(name)` provides an implicit `TableName` so `col(...)` calls inside it bind to that table; you subclass it as `object country extends TableDef("country")`. `RootDef` binds columns to the synthetic `<root>` table (TableName.rootName) for computed/aggregate root fields like `numCountries`.

keyConcepts.name: SqlField
keyConcepts.explanation: Maps a scalar GraphQL leaf field to a column. Flags: `key=true` marks an identity column used to group/assemble rows (an object mapping must have at least one key); `hidden=true` includes the column in SQL (e.g. for a join or discriminator) but omits it from GraphQL output; `discriminator=true` marks the column read by an interface/union discriminator; `associative=true` marks a key that is not a DB primary key (may repeat), e.g. a language code shared across rows.

keyConcepts.name: SqlObject + Join
keyConcepts.explanation: Maps a sub-object/list field. With no `Join`, the child object is *embedded* — it reuses the parent's table/row (e.g. a `Synopses` value built from columns on the `films` row). With one or more `Join`s, Grackle emits a SQL join from parent columns to child columns. `Join(parentCol, childCol)` is sugar for a single condition; `Join(List((p1,c1),(p2,c2)))` expresses composite-key joins; passing several `Join`s to `SqlObject(name, j1, j2, ...)` chains multi-table (associative-table) joins.

keyConcepts.name: SqlJson
keyConcepts.explanation: Maps a GraphQL object/interface field to a `jsonb` column. Unlike `SqlObject`, the JSON sub-tree below it is navigated entirely in-process by a `CirceCursor` — no further SQL is issued for nested selections, fragments, enums, arrays, or `__typename`. `SqlJson.subtree = true` signals that child selections are not SQL-mapped.

keyConcepts.name: Embedding vs joining
keyConcepts.explanation: Embedding = a GraphQL sub-object that lives on the same row as its parent (SqlObject with no Join, child SqlFields point at the parent's table). Joining = a sub-object on a different table reached via Join. The world mapping's `Country.cities` is a join; the embedding mapping's `Film.synopses` is embedded.

keyConcepts.name: PrefixedMapping for shared embedded types
keyConcepts.explanation: When one embedded GraphQL type (e.g. `Synopses`) is reached under multiple parents (films/synopses, series/synopses, episodes/synopses) and each parent stores it in a different table, you provide a `PrefixedMapping` keyed by the result-path prefix so each occurrence binds to the right table's columns.

keyConcepts.name: SqlInterfaceMapping + SqlDiscriminator
keyConcepts.explanation: An interface is mapped with `SqlInterfaceMapping(tpe, discriminator, fieldMappings)` over the shared/super-table; concrete subtypes are ordinary `ObjectMapping`s adding their extra columns on the same table. The `SqlDiscriminator` has `discriminate(cursor): Result[Type]` (compute concrete type of a fetched row) and `narrowPredicate(tpe): Result[Predicate]` (a WHERE predicate to select only rows of a given subtype). The discriminating column is an `SqlField(..., discriminator = true)`.

keyConcepts.name: SqlUnionMapping
keyConcepts.explanation: A union is mapped with `SqlUnionMapping(tpe, discriminator, fieldMappings)`. All members must share a table; the union mapping holds only hidden key + hidden discriminator fields; each member `ObjectMapping` maps its own column on the shared table. Union member field mappings must be hidden, and SqlJson/sub-object fields are not allowed directly in the union mapping.

keyConcepts.name: Doobie vs Skunk codecs
keyConcepts.explanation: The abstract `Codec` type is filled per backend. Doobie (`DoobieMappingLike`): `Codec = (Meta[_], Boolean)`, `Encoder = (Put[_], Boolean)`, `Fragment = doobie.Fragment`; `col(name, Meta[T], nullable=false)`. Skunk (`SkunkMappingLike`): `Codec = (skunk.Codec[_], Boolean)`, `Encoder = skunk.Encoder[_]`, `Fragment = skunk.AppliedFragment`; `col(name, skunk.Codec[T])` with nullability derived from `Option[T]` via implicit `IsNullable`. The boolean in each Codec tuple is the nullability flag.

keyConcepts.name: FailedJoin sentinel
keyConcepts.explanation: When an outer join produces no child row, non-nullable child columns decode to the `FailedJoin` case object rather than null, so Grackle can distinguish a genuinely-absent join target from a SQL NULL value.

keyTypes.name: SqlMappingLike
keyTypes.signature: trait SqlMappingLike[F[_]] extends CirceMappingLike[F] with SqlModule[F] { self =>
keyTypes.purpose: The database-agnostic core trait that defines all SQL field-mapping types (SqlField, SqlObject, SqlJson, Join, ColumnRef, TableDef, SqlInterfaceMapping, SqlUnionMapping, SqlDiscriminator) and the query-to-SQL compiler. Backend traits (DoobieMappingLike, SkunkMappingLike) extend it to supply Codec/Encoder/Fragment and `col`.

keyTypes.name: ColumnRef
keyTypes.signature: case class ColumnRef(table: String, column: String, codec: Codec, scalaTypeName: String, pos: SourcePos)
keyTypes.purpose: Reference to a single SQL column plus its codec; equality is by (table, column) only. Built via `col`, consumed by SqlField/SqlJson/Join.

keyTypes.name: TableDef
keyTypes.signature: class TableDef(name: String) { implicit val tableName: TableName = TableName(name) }
keyTypes.purpose: Base class for per-table column-definition objects; its implicit TableName binds enclosed `col(...)` calls to this table.

keyTypes.name: RootDef
keyTypes.signature: class RootDef { implicit val tableName: TableName = TableName.rootTableName }
keyTypes.purpose: Like TableDef but binds columns to the synthetic <root> table, for computed/aggregate root fields (e.g. numCountries).

keyTypes.name: SqlField

keyTypes.name: SqlObject
keyTypes.signature: case class SqlObject(fieldName: String, joins: List[Join])(implicit val pos: SourcePos) extends SqlFieldMapping  // companion: def apply(fieldName: String, joins: Join*)(implicit pos: SourcePos): SqlObject

keyTypes.name: SqlJson
keyTypes.signature: case class SqlJson(fieldName: String, columnRef: ColumnRef)(implicit val pos: SourcePos) extends SqlFieldMapping { def subtree = true }

keyTypes.name: Join
keyTypes.signature: case class Join(conditions: List[(ColumnRef, ColumnRef)])  // companion: def apply(parent: ColumnRef, child: ColumnRef): Join = new Join(List((parent, child)))

keyTypes.name: SqlDiscriminator
keyTypes.signature: trait SqlDiscriminator { def narrowPredicate(tpe: Type): Result[Predicate]; def discriminate(cursor: Cursor): Result[Type] }

keyTypes.name: SqlInterfaceMapping
keyTypes.signature: sealed trait SqlInterfaceMapping extends ObjectMapping with SqlDiscriminatedType  // object SqlInterfaceMapping { def apply(tpe: NamedType, discriminator: SqlDiscriminator)(fieldMappings: FieldMapping*)(implicit pos): ObjectMapping ; def apply(tpe: NamedType, fieldMappings: List[FieldMapping], discriminator: SqlDiscriminator)(implicit pos): ObjectMapping ; def apply(path: Path, discriminator: SqlDiscriminator)(fieldMappings: FieldMapping*) ; def apply(predicate: MappingPredicate, discriminator: SqlDiscriminator)(fieldMappings: FieldMapping*) }

keyTypes.name: SqlUnionMapping

keyTypes.name: DoobieMappingLike
keyTypes.signature: trait DoobieMappingLike[F[_]] extends Mapping[F] with SqlMappingLike[F] { type Codec = (Meta[_], Boolean); type Encoder = (Put[_], Boolean); type Fragment = DoobieFragment ; def col[T](colName: String, codec: Meta[T], nullable: Boolean = false)(implicit tableName: TableName, typeName: TypeName[T], pos: SourcePos): ColumnRef }

keyTypes.name: SkunkMappingLike

minimalExamples.explanation: Doobie's `col` is `col(name, Meta[T], nullable = Boolean)`; Skunk's `col(name, skunk.Codec[T])` derives nullability from whether the codec is for `Option[T]`. The doobie example is from demo/world/WorldMapping.scala; the skunk codec helpers from SkunkDatabaseSuite.scala.

gotchas: Every object type mapping must declare at least one `key = true` field (direct or inherited), or validation fails with `NoKeyInObjectTypeMapping` ("Object type mappings must include at least one direct or inherited key field mapping").

All SqlField/SqlObject columns of a single (non-interface/non-union) object type mapping must come from the same table, otherwise `SplitObjectTypeMapping`/`SplitEmbeddedObjectTypeMapping` fails. To span tables, use `SqlObject` + `Join` (a sub-object) instead.

Interface and union subtypes must all be mapped onto the SAME shared table as the interface/union mapping; the subtype ObjectMappings only add extra columns on that table. `SplitInterfaceTypeMapping`/`SplitUnionTypeMapping` reject splitting across tables.

In a union mapping every member field mapping must be hidden (`NonHiddenUnionFieldMapping`), and you cannot put `SqlObject` sub-objects (`IllegalSubobjectInUnionTypeMapping`) or `SqlJson` fields (`IllegalJsonInUnionTypeMapping`) directly in the union mapping — map those on the member ObjectMappings.
An interface/union mapping must have a discriminator field, and the discriminator field must not be polymorphic: `NoDiscriminatorInObjectTypeMapping` / `IllegalPolymorphicDiscriminatorFieldMapping`.

`associative = true` is only valid on a key field; an associative non-key triggers `AssocFieldNotKey`. Use it for keys that aren't DB primary keys and can repeat (e.g. `Language.language` shared across countries) so rows group correctly.

`ColumnRef` equality and hashCode use only (table, column) — the codec is ignored. Referencing the same physical column with two different codecs yields 'equal' ColumnRefs, which can mask codec mismatches.

Join requires conditions: `SqlObject("x", Join(...))` with an empty condition list fails `NoJoinConditions`; chained multi-Join SqlObjects must have parent->child tables that line up or you get `MisalignedJoins` / `InconsistentJoinConditions`.
`SqlObject(name)` with NO Join means *embedding* (child reuses parent's row/table), which is easy to confuse with a join. If you intend a separate table you must pass a `Join`.

Under `SqlJson`, nested fields are resolved from the decoded JSON in-process, not via SQL — so you cannot join out of, filter on, or order by fields inside a jsonb sub-tree; they behave like a Circe value mapping. A non-nullable SqlJson field whose column is actually NULL/absent will error ('expected jsonb value').

Doobie and Skunk differ in how nullability is specified: doobie `col(name, Meta[T], nullable = true)` vs skunk `col(name, codec.opt)` (inferred from Option[T]). The Codec is a `(codec, Boolean)` tuple in both, where the Boolean is the nullability flag.
Failed outer joins decode non-nullable child columns to the `FailedJoin` sentinel object (not null); code that inspects raw row arrays must account for it.

When the same GraphQL embedded type appears under multiple parents in different tables, a plain ObjectMapping is ambiguous — you must use `PrefixedMapping` keyed by the result-path prefix (e.g. List("films","synopses")).

Hidden columns (`hidden = true`) are still fetched and used for joins/keys/discriminators but omitted from the GraphQL response; forgetting `hidden = true` on join/discriminator columns leaks them or pollutes the schema-vs-mapping consistency checks.

summary: Grackle has no dedicated "mutation runtime" — GraphQL mutations are modelled as ordinary root fields on the schema's `Mutation` type whose field mappings are `RootEffect`s. A `RootEffect` is an `EffectMapping` that runs an effect `F[Result[(Query, Cursor)]]` before the normal result-construction stage: it performs the effectful write and then yields the (possibly rewritten) query plus a root cursor that the interpreter traverses to build the response. Three convenience constructors cover the common shapes: `RootEffect.computeUnit` (write, leave the query/cursor unchanged), `RootEffect.computeCursor` (write, supply a hand-built cursor — used by in-memory mappings), and `RootEffect.computeChild` (write, then rewrite the child query using data only known after the write, e.g. a freshly-inserted row id). Arguments reach the effect via the elaboration `Env` (populated in the `SelectElaborator` with `Elab.env(...)` and read with `env.getR[...]`). Mutations execute serially in client order within a single `runOneShot` pass; `RootEffect` and `RootStream` share machinery, with `RootStream` reserved for subscriptions. Grackle itself does not open or manage transactions — atomicity is entirely the responsibility of the user's effect (e.g. doobie `.transact(xa)` or a skunk session).

keyConcepts.name: RootEffect
keyConcepts.explanation: An `EffectMapping` field mapping placed on the schema's `Mutation` (or `Query`) object type. It wraps `effect: (Query, Path, Env) => F[Result[(Query, Cursor)]]`. The interpreter runs this effect first (the actual write), then traverses the returned cursor with the returned query to construct the JSON response. This is the entire mechanism behind GraphQL mutations in Grackle — there is no separate mutation API.

keyConcepts.name: computeUnit / computeCursor / computeChild
keyConcepts.explanation: The three convenience constructors on `object RootEffect`. `computeUnit` runs an `Env => F[Result[Unit]]` effect and reuses the default root cursor with the unmodified (elaborated) query — used when the elaborator already rewrote the query (e.g. an UPDATE keyed on an id supplied as an argument). `computeChild` runs `(Query, Path, Env) => F[Result[Query]]`, letting you rewrite the child query *after* the effect — essential when the row id only exists post-INSERT. `computeCursor` runs `(Path, Env) => F[Result[Cursor]]` and supplies a hand-built cursor (e.g. `valueCursor`), used by in-memory ValueMappings and subscriptions.

keyConcepts.name: Env-based argument passing
keyConcepts.explanation: Mutation arguments are not passed directly to the effect. Instead the `SelectElaborator` captures them into the elaboration environment with `Elab.env(name, value)`; the value is later retrieved inside the `RootEffect` body with `env.getR[T](name)` (a `Result[T]`) or `env.get[T](name)` (an `Option[T]`). The interpreter merges per-node environments into the effect's `Env` via `rootCursor.fullEnv.addFromQuery(query)`.

keyConcepts.name: Two-phase elaboration for inserts
keyConcepts.explanation: For an UPDATE the client query can be fully elaborated up front (the `id` is an argument), so `computeUnit` + an elaborator `transformChild` that adds `Unique(Filter(Eql(.../"id", Const(id)), child))` suffices. For an INSERT the new row's `id` is unknown until the write runs, so the query rewrite must happen *inside* the effect via `computeChild`, which returns `Unique(Filter(Eql(CityType / "id", Const(id)), child)).success` using the id returned by the INSERT.

keyConcepts.name: Serial execution of mutation roots
keyConcepts.explanation: In `QueryInterpreter.runOneShot`, ungrouped root selections are partitioned into effectful (RootEffect-backed) and pure queries. Effectful queries are run with `effectfulQueries.traverse { ... }`, which for `F = IO` executes them sequentially in client order — matching the GraphQL spec requirement that top-level mutation fields run serially (verified by the 'serial execution' test). Results are merged with `|+|`.

keyConcepts.name: Transactions are the user's responsibility
keyConcepts.explanation: Grackle does not begin/commit transactions around a mutation. The `RootEffect` effect value is whatever the user supplies; the doobie test wraps each write in `.transact(transactor)` and the skunk test uses `pool.use(_.prepareR(...))`. Atomicity across the write and the subsequent read-back is therefore not guaranteed by Grackle and must be arranged by the user if required.

keyConcepts.name: RootStream vs RootEffect
keyConcepts.explanation: `RootStream` is the streaming sibling of `RootEffect` (effect type returns `Stream[F, Result[(Query, Cursor)]]`) and is only permitted in subscriptions; `runOneShot` returns an internal error if a `RootStream` appears in a non-subscription. A `RootEffect` can be lifted to a single-element stream via `toRootStream`, which is how subscriptions fall back to a plain effect when no explicit `RootStream` is defined.

gotchas: RootEffect's case-class constructor is private. You MUST use the companion factories (`RootEffect.apply`, `computeUnit`, `computeCursor`, `computeChild`) — you cannot `new RootEffect(...)` from user code.

Arguments are NOT passed to the effect directly. They flow through the elaboration Env: bind them in the `SelectElaborator` with `Elab.env(name, value)` and read them in the effect with `env.getR[T](name)` / `env.get[T](name)`. Forgetting the `Elab.env` step makes `env.getR` fail at runtime with 'Key ... of type ... was not found'.

Choosing the wrong constructor for inserts: for an UPDATE keyed on an argument you can elaborate the read-back query up front (`computeUnit` + `transformChild`), but for an INSERT whose id is generated by the DB you MUST use `computeChild` and rewrite the query inside the effect — the id does not exist at elaboration time. The test comments call this out explicitly ('the query must be elaborated *after* execution of the effect').

Grackle does not manage transactions. There is no implicit transaction wrapping the write plus the subsequent read-back. The doobie tests use `.transact(transactor)` per statement and the skunk tests use `pool.use(...)`; if you need the write and read-back to be atomic you must arrange that yourself. The two halves can run on different connections/transactions.

computeChild requires the root query to have a recognisable shape. Internally it uses `Query.extractChild` / `Query.substChild`; if the top-level selection isn't a plain `Select`/`UntypedSelect` (optionally wrapped in `Environment`/`TransformCursor`) you get 'Root query has unexpected shape' errors.

`RootStream` is rejected outside subscriptions: `runOneShot` returns 'RootStream only permitted in subscriptions', and conversely subscriptions require an `EffectMapping` ('EffectMapping required for subscriptions'). Don't put a `RootStream` on the Mutation type.

Top-level mutation fields execute serially in client order (per the GraphQL spec). This is implied by `effectfulQueries.traverse` in `runOneShot` and is asserted by the 'serial execution' test (one:put / two:put / three:put leaves the ref at 3). Do not assume parallelism between sibling mutation roots.

`env.getR[T]` returns a `Result[T]` (an error value), not a thrown exception, when the key/type is missing — so you must sequence it (`.traverse`/`.flatTraverse`) rather than pattern-matching as if it were the raw value. `env.get[T]` returns `Option[T]` and silently yields `None` on type mismatch (it uses `classTag[T].unapply`).

The SQL mutation tests deliberately operate on a *copy* table `city_copy` (created via `CREATE TABLE city_copy AS SELECT * FROM city` and dropped afterwards) so the writes don't corrupt the shared read-only `city` fixture. The TableDef is `TableDef("city_copy")` while the GraphQL type is still `City`.

`computeCursor` leaves the client query unmodified, so any data produced by the effect can only reach result construction via the cursor's environment (`qc.map(_.withEnv(env))` / `valueCursor(path, env, value)`). If you build a cursor that doesn't carry the written value, the response won't reflect it.

summary: Grackle implements GraphQL subscriptions by allowing the root fields of the schema's `Subscription` type to be mapped to `RootStream` field mappings, whose effect produces an `fs2.Stream` of results rather than a single value. Each element emitted by the stream re-runs the rest of the subscription query (the "child" selection) and produces one GraphQL JSON response, so the public entry point `Mapping#compileAndRunSubscription` returns an `fs2.Stream[F, Json]` that emits one JSON document per upstream event. A `RootStream` can compute a stream of cursors directly (`RootStream.computeCursor`), a stream of effect-specific child queries that are executed against the mapping's default root cursor (`RootStream.computeChild`), or both query and cursor (`RootStream.apply`); a plain `RootEffect` is also accepted in a subscription position and is automatically lifted via `toRootStream` (emitting exactly one element). The skunk backend demonstrates the canonical pattern: a Postgres `LISTEN`/`NOTIFY` channel (`Session#channel(...).listen(...)`) drives the stream, and each notification carries an id used to build a `Unique(Filter(...))` child query that fetches the affected row. Subscriptions are restricted to exactly one root selection and `RootStream` is only legal under the `Subscription` operation type — using it elsewhere (or returning more than one root selection) is a runtime internal error.

keyConcepts.name: RootStream (stream-valued root)
keyConcepts.explanation: An `EffectMapping` placed on a `Subscription` root field whose `effect` returns an `fs2.Stream[F, Result[(Query, Cursor)]]`. Each emitted element drives one full re-interpretation of the subscription's child selection, yielding one response. This is the core mechanism that turns a single GraphQL subscription operation into a stream of JSON responses.

keyConcepts.name: compileAndRunSubscription
keyConcepts.explanation: The public Mapping method that compiles a subscription (or any operation) and returns `Stream[F, Json]`. For a `Subscription` operation it dispatches to `runSubscription`; for `Query`/`Mutation` it produces a single-element stream. `compileAndRun` is implemented on top of it by collecting the stream and asserting exactly one element, so mutations/queries reuse the same machinery.

keyConcepts.name: computeCursor vs computeChild vs apply
keyConcepts.explanation: Three ways to build a RootStream. `computeCursor(field)((path, env) => Stream[F, Result[Cursor]])` emits cursors and leaves the elaborated client query unchanged (used when the data is materialised in-process, e.g. ValueMapping/Circe). `computeChild(field)((child, path, env) => Stream[F, Result[Query]])` emits a transformed child query that is run against the mapping's default root cursor (used by SQL backends so each event re-queries the DB). `apply(field)(effect)` gives full control over both query and cursor.

keyConcepts.name: RootEffect.toRootStream lifting
keyConcepts.explanation: A `RootEffect` (used for queries/mutations) placed in a subscription position is accepted and wrapped via `toRootStream`, which lifts its single `F[Result[(Query,Cursor)]]` into a one-element stream with `Stream.eval`. So a subscription field need not literally be a RootStream, though RootStream is the idiomatic choice.

keyConcepts.name: Postgres LISTEN/NOTIFY via skunk
keyConcepts.explanation: The recommended real-data subscription source: `Session#channel(id"...")` gives a skunk `Channel`; `.listen(maxQueued)` yields an `fs2.Stream` of notifications and `.notify(payload)` publishes. In Grackle the listen stream lives inside a `RootStream.computeChild` body (opened via `fs2.Stream.resource(pool)`), and each notification's payload (a city id here) is used to build a `Unique(Filter(Eql(CityType / "id", Const(id)), child))` query that fetches and emits the changed row.

keyConcepts.name: Single root selection / Subscription-only restriction
keyConcepts.explanation: Subscriptions permit exactly one root field selection (more than one is an internal error). Conversely a `RootStream` is only legal under the Subscription type — encountering one while running a non-subscription operation is also an internal error. These invariants are enforced in `QueryInterpreter.runSubscription`/`runOneShot`.

minimalExamples.title: In-process subscription with ValueMapping + SignallingRef
minimalExamples.code:
import scala.concurrent.duration._
import cats.effect._
import cats.implicits._
import fs2.concurrent.SignallingRef
import io.circe.Json
import grackle._
import grackle.QueryCompiler._
import grackle.syntax._

def mapping(ref: SignallingRef[IO, Int]): Mapping[IO] =
  new ValueMapping[IO] {
    val schema: Schema =
      schema"""
        type Query        { get: Int! }
        type Mutation     { put(n: Int): Int! }
        type Subscription { watch: Int! }
      """

    val QueryType        = schema.ref("Query")
    val MutationType     = schema.ref("Mutation")
    val SubscriptionType = schema.ref("Subscription")

    val typeMappings = List(
      ObjectMapping(QueryType, List(
        RootEffect.computeCursor("get")((path, env) =>
          ref.get.map(n => Result(valueCursor(path, env, n)))))),
      ObjectMapping(MutationType, List(
        RootEffect.computeCursor("put")((path, env) =>
          env.get[Int]("n") match {
            case None    => Result.failure(s"`n: Int` not found in $env").pure[IO]
            case Some(n) => ref.set(n).map(_ => Result(valueCursor(path, env, n)))
          }))),
      ObjectMapping(SubscriptionType, List(
        // stream-valued root: one response per distinct value
        RootStream.computeCursor("watch")((path, env) =>
          ref.discrete.map(n => Result(valueCursor(path, env, n))))))
    )

    override val selectElaborator: SelectElaborator = SelectElaborator {
      case (MutationType, "put", List(Query.Binding("n", Value.IntValue(n)))) =>
        Elab.env("n" -> n)
    }
  }

// Run: subscribe in a fiber, mutate, collect emissions.
val prog: IO[List[Json]] =
  for {
    ref <- SignallingRef[IO, Int](0)
    map  = mapping(ref)
    fib <- map.compileAndRunSubscription("subscription { watch }")
             .take(4).compile.toList.start
    _ <- IO.sleep(100.milli)
    _ <- map.compileAndRun("mutation { put(n: 123) }")
    _ <- IO.sleep(100.milli)
    _ <- map.compileAndRun("mutation { put(n: 42) }")
    _ <- IO.sleep(100.milli)
    _ <- map.compileAndRun("mutation { put(n: 77) }")
    _ <- IO.sleep(100.milli)
    out <- fib.join
    res <- out.embedNever
  } yield res
// res == [ {watch:0}, {watch:123}, {watch:42}, {watch:77} ] (wrapped in {"data": ...})
minimalExamples.explanation: The complete in-process subscription pattern, taken verbatim from modules/core/src/test/scala/subscription/SubscriptionSuite.scala. `RootStream.computeCursor` wires the `watch` subscription field to `ref.discrete` (an fs2.Stream of the SignallingRef's values); each emitted value becomes one `{"data":{"watch": n}}` response. `valueCursor(path, env, n)` builds the cursor for the leaf result. Note the explicit `IO.sleep` between mutations: subscription delivery is asynchronous and the test races the subscriber against the producer. `embedNever` is fs2's helper for unwrapping the fiber Outcome.

minimalExamples.title: Postgres LISTEN/NOTIFY subscription via skunk (RootStream.computeChild)
minimalExamples.explanation: The complete Postgres LISTEN/NOTIFY worked example, assembled verbatim from modules/skunk/js-jvm/src/test/scala/subscription/SubscriptionMapping.scala and SubscriptionSuite.scala. The subscription source is `s.channel(id"city_channel").listen(256)` — an fs2.Stream of skunk notifications opened over a session from `pool` (the SkunkMapping's connection pool). Each notification's `.value` (a stringified city id) is parsed and used to build `Unique(Filter(Eql(CityType / "id", Const(id)), child))`, where `child` is the elaborated `{ name country { name } }` selection; Grackle then issues the SQL to read that city and emits one response per NOTIFY. `.success` lifts the Query into `Result[Query]`. The driver publishes with `channel(...).contramap[Int](_.toString).notify(...)`. The `IO.sleep(1.second)` avoids a race where notifications fire before LISTEN is registered.

minimalExamples.title: Circe-backed stream root via RootStream.computeJson
minimalExamples.explanation: When the data is already Circe JSON (or has a circe Encoder), `RootStream.computeJson` / `computeEncodable` (added by the implicit `CirceMappingRootStreamSyntax` in modules/circe/src/main/scala/circemapping.scala) build a RootStream directly from a `Stream[F, Result[Json]]`/`Stream[F, Result[A]]`, internally delegating to `computeCursor` with `circeCursor`. Mirrors the RootEffect.computeJson/computeEncodable helpers used for query/mutation roots.

gotchas: Subscriptions allow exactly one root selection. `runSubscription` returns `Result.internalError("Only one root selection permitted for subscriptions")` if the operation selects more than one top-level field (see modules/core/src/main/scala/queryinterpreter.scala).

A `RootStream` is only valid under the `Subscription` operation type. If a query/mutation reaches a RootStream-mapped field, `runOneShot` short-circuits with `Result.internalError("RootStream only permitted in subscriptions")`. Conversely, a subscription field with no RootStream/RootEffect yields `"EffectMapping required for subscriptions"`.

`compileAndRun` (for queries/mutations) is built on `compileAndRunSubscription` and asserts the result stream has exactly one element — it raises IllegalStateException("Result stream was empty.") on an empty stream or "...contained N results; expected exactly one." otherwise. Don't point it at a true subscription.

Delivery is asynchronous and racy. Both test suites insert `IO.sleep` (100ms in core, 1s for Postgres) between starting the subscriber fiber and producing events, because the subscriber must attach (and, for Postgres, register LISTEN) before notifications are sent. The core suite even comments "this is the best we can do for now". Production code must account for this ordering window; events fired before the listener is ready are lost.

`RootStream.computeChild`'s effect receives the already-elaborated `child` selection (not the full root query) and must return a `Result[Query]` that wraps/extends it; in the skunk example it wraps `child` in `Unique(Filter(...))`. Returning a query of the wrong shape, or failing to incorporate `child`, breaks the result. `extractChild`/`substChild` are used internally and an unexpected query shape yields `Result.internalError("Root query has unexpected shape")`.

`RootStream.apply`, `computeCursor` and `computeChild` share an erased signature, so the `apply` overload carries a `DummyImplicit` to disambiguate. Use the named `computeCursor`/`computeChild`/`computeJson` helpers in user code to avoid overload-resolution surprises.

The Postgres `Channel` payload is always a String. In the skunk example the producer does `channel(id"city_channel").contramap[Int](_.toString).notify(...)` and the consumer does `.listen(256).map(_.value.toInt)`. You are responsible for encoding/parsing the payload yourself; there is no typed channel.

`Session#channel(...).listen(maxQueued)` takes a bounded queue size (256 in the example). Notifications beyond the buffer while the consumer is slow can be dropped by skunk — choose the bound deliberately.

For SQL subscriptions you open a *new* session for the LISTEN stream via `fs2.Stream.resource(pool)` inside the RootStream body; the per-event child query then runs against the mapping's own pool. Each emitted event triggers a fresh SQL round-trip (re-querying the row), so a high notification rate means high query load.

Mutations within a single GraphQL mutation operation execute serially in selection order (see the "serial execution" test putting n:1, n:2, n:3). This matters when a mutation is the producer feeding a subscription — ordering of resulting subscription emissions follows the serialized mutations, but only up to the async delivery window above.

summary: Grackle's effects subsystem lets a Mapping run side-effecting computations (database queries, HTTP calls, ref updates, etc.) at two distinct points in query execution. RootEffect / RootStream attach an effect to a top-level Query/Mutation/Subscription field; they run once, up front, before the rest of the query is interpreted, and yield an effect-specific Query plus root Cursor. EffectField + EffectHandler attach an effect to a nested field deep inside the result tree; the EffectElaborator compiler phase wraps such fields in an Effect algebra node, and the interpreter defers every occurrence of that node into a ProtoJson.EffectJson placeholder. At the end of a stage the interpreter gathers all deferred EffectJson values and groups them by (mapping, handler), so a single EffectHandler.runEffects call receives a List[(Query, Cursor)] for every instance of that field across the whole result — this is the batching mechanism that turns a would-be N+1 into one call. The handler runs the effect once, produces one continuation Cursor per input pair, and the interpreter then evaluates each continuation child query against its cursor and scatters the JSON back into the original result tree. The circe and sql modules add convenience constructors (computeJson, computeEncodable) and reusable handlers built on Cursor/Json.

keyConcepts.name: RootEffect (root effects)
keyConcepts.explanation: A FieldMapping for a top-level field that runs an effect once, before the rest of the query is interpreted, returning F[Result[(Query, Cursor)]]. Used for mutation side effects and per-query setup. In runOneShot the interpreter partitions root queries into effectful vs pure; effectful ones run their RootEffect first, then runValue against the returned (query, cursor). Convenience constructors (computeUnit/computeCursor/computeChild) cover the common cases of computing just the cursor, just the child query, or neither.

keyConcepts.name: RootStream (subscriptions)
keyConcepts.explanation: The streaming analogue of RootEffect: effect returns Stream[F, Result[(Query, Cursor)]], emitting one result per stream element. Only permitted in subscriptions — runOneShot raises an internal error 'RootStream only permitted in subscriptions' if one is reached for a query/mutation. RootEffect.toRootStream lifts a RootEffect into a single-element RootStream so mutations can be served through the subscription path.

keyConcepts.name: EffectField + EffectHandler (nested/deferred effects)
keyConcepts.explanation: EffectField is a FieldMapping for a nested field; it names an EffectHandler[F] and an optional list of required sibling columns. EffectHandler has one method runEffects(queries: List[(Query, Cursor)]): F[Result[List[Cursor]]]. The handler receives one (continuation-query, parent-cursor) pair per occurrence of the field in the result and must return one continuation Cursor per pair, in the same order.

keyConcepts.name: Effect algebra node
keyConcepts.explanation: case class Effect[F[_]](handler: EffectHandler[F], child: Query). The EffectElaborator compiler phase rewrites Select(field, _, child) into Select(field, _, Effect(handler, Select(field,_,child))) wherever an EffectField mapping exists for that field. At interpretation, Select(_, _, Effect(handler, cont)) is turned into a deferred ProtoJson.effect(...) placeholder rather than being evaluated inline.

keyConcepts.name: Batching via groupMap
keyConcepts.explanation: In completeAll, all deferred EffectJson placeholders are gathered across the entire ProtoJson tree and grouped with .groupMap(ej => (ej.mapping, ej.handler))(identity). Each group becomes exactly one handler.runEffects call carrying the full batch of (query, cursor) pairs. This is what collapses N sibling/nested effect fields into a single service call (avoiding N+1).

keyConcepts.name: Two-stage interpretation
keyConcepts.explanation: Interpretation proceeds in stages. A stage produces a ProtoJson that may contain deferred EffectJson nodes; completeAll runs the deferred effects (the next stage), evaluates their continuation child queries against the returned cursors, and scatters the resulting Json back into placeholders by identity. Each effect field therefore costs one extra stage, but all instances of it share that stage.

keyConcepts.name: required columns
keyConcepts.explanation: EffectField(fieldName, handler, required, hidden). 'required' lists sibling fields/columns that must be fetched in the parent query so the handler can read them from the parent Cursor (e.g. List("code2") so CurrencyQueryHandler can call parentCursor.fieldAs[String]("code2")). In SqlMapping this drives columnsForLeaf so the SQL SELECT includes those columns.

keyConcepts.name: childContext / continuation query
keyConcepts.explanation: The Query passed to a handler is the continuation child (the selection set under the effect field). Query.childContext(parentCursor.context, query) derives the GraphQL Context for the result the handler must produce, and Query.extractChild is used by the interpreter to get the inner query that is finally run against each returned cursor.

keyTypes.name: Effect
keyTypes.signature: case class Effect[F[_]](handler: EffectHandler[F], child: Query) extends Query { def render = s"<effect: ${child.render}>" }
keyTypes.purpose: Algebra node that embeds a possibly-batched deferred effect. Inserted by EffectElaborator around fields backed by an EffectField; the interpreter defers it into a ProtoJson.EffectJson placeholder.

keyTypes.name: EffectHandler
keyTypes.signature: trait EffectHandler[F[_]] { def runEffects(queries: List[(Query, Cursor)]): F[Result[List[Cursor]]] }
keyTypes.purpose: User-implemented strategy that runs the batched effect for all occurrences of a nested effect field and returns one continuation Cursor per input pair (same order).

keyTypes.name: EffectMapping
keyTypes.signature: trait EffectMapping extends FieldMapping { def subtree: Boolean = true }
keyTypes.purpose: Common supertype of EffectField, RootEffect, and RootStream. subtree = true marks the field as owning its whole subtree.

keyTypes.name: EffectField
keyTypes.signature: case class EffectField(fieldName: String, handler: EffectHandler[F], required: List[String] = Nil, hidden: Boolean = false)(implicit val pos: SourcePos) extends EffectMapping
keyTypes.purpose: FieldMapping that attaches an EffectHandler to a nested field, optionally declaring sibling columns ('required') that must be present in the parent so the handler can read them from the parent Cursor.

keyTypes.name: RootEffect
keyTypes.signature: case class RootEffect private (fieldName: String, effect: (Query, Path, Env) => F[Result[(Query, Cursor)]])(implicit val pos: SourcePos) extends EffectMapping { def hidden = false; def toRootStream: RootStream = RootStream(fieldName)((q, p, e) => Stream.eval(effect(q, p, e))) }
keyTypes.purpose: FieldMapping for a top-level field that runs an effect once before interpretation, returning a possibly-modified Query and a root Cursor. Primary constructor is private; use the companion object factories.

keyTypes.name: RootEffect.apply
keyTypes.signature: def apply(fieldName: String)(effect: (Query, Path, Env) => F[Result[(Query, Cursor)]])(implicit pos: SourcePos, di: DummyImplicit): RootEffect
keyTypes.purpose: Full-control constructor: perform an initial effect and yield both an effect-specific query and its corresponding root cursor.

keyTypes.name: RootEffect.computeUnit
keyTypes.signature: def computeUnit(fieldName: String)(effect: Env => F[Result[Unit]])(implicit pos: SourcePos): RootEffect
keyTypes.purpose: Run a pure side effect (e.g. a mutation write) leaving the query and default root cursor unchanged; effect results can only be propagated via the Env.

keyTypes.name: RootEffect.computeCursor
keyTypes.signature: def computeCursor(fieldName: String)(effect: (Path, Env) => F[Result[Cursor]])(implicit pos: SourcePos): RootEffect
keyTypes.purpose: Run an effect and yield a custom root Cursor; the (elaborated) client query is used unchanged. Used by ValueMapping/CirceMapping examples (valueCursor/circeCursor).

keyTypes.name: RootEffect.computeChild
keyTypes.signature: def computeChild(fieldName: String)(effect: (Query, Path, Env) => F[Result[Query]])(implicit pos: SourcePos): RootEffect
keyTypes.purpose: Run an effect that computes a replacement child query, which is then executed against the mapping's default root cursor (e.g. to inject a Filter/Limit derived from the effect).

keyTypes.name: RootStream
keyTypes.signature: case class RootStream private (fieldName: String, effect: (Query, Path, Env) => Stream[F, Result[(Query, Cursor)]])(implicit val pos: SourcePos) extends EffectMapping { def hidden = false }
keyTypes.purpose: Streaming root effect used for subscriptions; companion provides apply/computeCursor/computeChild mirroring RootEffect but returning Stream.

keyTypes.name: EffectElaborator
keyTypes.signature: class EffectElaborator[F[_]] private (effects: (Context, String) => Option[EffectHandler[F]]) extends Phase { override def transform(query: Query): Elab[Query] = ... case Some(handler) => Select(fieldName, resultName, Effect(handler, s.copy(child = ec))) ... }
keyTypes.purpose: Compiler phase (added by Mapping.compilerPhases after selectElaborator and componentElaborator) that wraps each effect-mapped field's Select in an Effect node so the interpreter defers it.

keyTypes.name: ProtoJson.effect
keyTypes.signature: def effect[F[_]](mapping: Mapping[F], handler: EffectHandler[F], query: Query, cursor: Cursor): ProtoJson = wrap(EffectJson(mapping, Some(handler), query, cursor))
keyTypes.purpose: Builds the deferred placeholder for one occurrence of a nested effect field; collected and batched in completeAll.

keyTypes.name: QueryInterpreter.completeAll
keyTypes.signature: def completeAll[F[_]: Monad](pjs: List[ProtoJson]): F[Result[List[Json]]]
keyTypes.purpose: Gathers all deferred EffectJson across the ProtoJson tree, groups by (mapping, handler) into single runEffects batches, evaluates each continuation, and scatters results back by identity. This is where N+1 collapsing happens.

keyTypes.name: Mapping.combineAndRun
keyTypes.signature: def combineAndRun(queries: List[(Query, Cursor)]): F[Result[List[ProtoJson]]]
keyTypes.purpose: Default batch runner for component (mapping-delegated) deferrals; overridable so e.g. SQL mappings can combine queries. EffectHandler-based deferrals bypass this and call handler.runEffects directly.

keyTypes.name: Query.childContext
keyTypes.signature: def childContext(c: Context, query: Query): Result[Context]
keyTypes.purpose: Derives the child GraphQL Context for the continuation query inside a handler (used by CurrencyQueryHandler to build CirceCursor children).

gotchas: EffectHandler.runEffects must return EXACTLY one Cursor per input (Query, Cursor) pair, in the SAME order. The interpreter does (conts, cs).parMapN and scatters by position; a mismatched length or order silently corrupts results. The SQL examples go to real effort (indices + sortBy(_._2)) to restore the original order after grouping.

Batching key is (mapping, handler) identity. In completeAll the grouping is .groupMap(ej => (ej.mapping, ej.handler)). To get a single batched call you must reuse the SAME handler object instance across all occurrences (e.g. `object CurrencyQueryHandler extends EffectHandler[F]`). Constructing a fresh handler per field or per row would split the batch and reintroduce N+1.

'required' columns are mandatory for nested handlers that read parent data. EffectField("currencies", handler, List("code2")) makes the parent SQL SELECT include code2; without it parentCursor.fieldAs[String]("code2") fails. In SqlMapping this is wired through columnsForLeaf (case Some(EffectField(_, _, required, _))).

RootStream is only valid in subscriptions. runOneShot checks hasRootStream and returns Result.internalError("RootStream only permitted in subscriptions") for a normal query/mutation. Conversely, mutations served via the subscription path use RootEffect.toRootStream to lift a single-shot effect into a one-element stream.

Each distinct nested effect field costs an extra interpreter stage. The effect is deferred into a ProtoJson placeholder and only resolved in completeAll. Doubly-nested effects (Currency.country inside Country.currencies) therefore run in successive stages — correct, but be aware the handler's continuation query is itself interpreted as a fresh sub-run.

The Query handed to a handler is the CONTINUATION CHILD, not the original field select. Handlers must use Query.childContext(parentCursor.context, query) / Query.extractChild to derive the right context and inner query. The interpreter also calls Query.extractChild on each input and errors with "Continuation query has the wrong shape" if a handler returns a cursor whose query isn't a single Select-shaped child.

RootEffect.computeUnit and computeCursor leave the client query unchanged; the ONLY channel to pass effect results downstream is the Env attached to the returned Cursor (the constructors call qc.map(_.withEnv(env))). If you need to change what is queried, use computeChild (which substitutes the child query) or the full RootEffect.apply.

RootEffect's primary constructor is private — you must go through the companion factories (apply / computeUnit / computeCursor / computeChild), or the circe-specific computeJson / computeEncodable from CirceMappingRootEffectSyntax. The bare apply also needs a DummyImplicit to disambiguate its overloads.

Independent root fields each fire their own RootEffect. The 'circe effect (multiple)' test (foo+bar+baz) ends with the counter at 3, not 1 — root effects are NOT batched across sibling root fields; only nested EffectField occurrences are batched.

summary: Grackle lets you stitch several independent `Mapping`s together behind a single GraphQL schema. A parent mapping extends `ComposedMapping[F]` and, for any field whose subtree should be served by another mapping, uses a `Delegate(fieldName, otherMapping, join)` field mapping instead of a normal value/SQL field mapping. At query-compile time the `componentElaborator` phase rewrites each delegated `Select` into a `Component(otherMapping, join, child)` query node marking a component boundary. At interpretation time the parent runs its part of the query, then the `join` function is applied to the parent's `Cursor` and the delegated child query to produce a continuation query (e.g. turning `country { currency }` into `fx(code: country.currencyCode)`); that continuation is deferred as a `ProtoJson.component`, grouped by target mapping in `completeAll`, and executed in a later stage by the other mapping's interpreter via its `combineAndRun`. This is the mechanism behind cross-mapping joins such as a SQL-backed `world` schema joined to an in-memory/effectful `currencies` mapping, and it composes recursively and supports per-mapping query batching by overriding `combineAndRun`.

keyConcepts.name: ComposedMapping[F]
keyConcepts.explanation: Base class a parent/root mapping extends to delegate subtrees to other mappings. Its only real job is overriding mkCursorForMappedField to produce a ComposedCursor (a placeholder cursor with focus = null and parent = None) for delegated fields, because the parent has no local data for them. It still needs its own schema, typeMappings and selectElaborator. Defined in modules/core/src/main/scala/composedmapping.scala.

keyConcepts.name: Delegate (field mapping)
keyConcepts.explanation: A FieldMapping (member of Mapping, used inside an ObjectMapping's fieldMappings) of the form Delegate(fieldName, mapping, join). It declares that fieldName on this object type is served by another Mapping. hidden=false, subtree=true. The optional join defaults to ComponentElaborator.TrivialJoin (pass the child query through unchanged). Defined in modules/core/src/main/scala/mapping.scala.

keyConcepts.name: join function
keyConcepts.explanation: A (Query, Cursor) => Result[Query] supplied to Delegate. Given the delegated child Query and the parent's Cursor (focused on the parent object), it returns the continuation Query the OTHER mapping will run. This is where a cross-mapping JOIN is expressed: you pattern-match the parent's focus (e.g. a Country case class) and rewrite Select("currency", child) into Select("fx", Unique(Filter(Eql(.../code, Const(country.currencyCode)), child))). Returning a Group(...) of selects produces a list result (one delegated query per id).

keyConcepts.name: Component query node
keyConcepts.explanation: case class Component[F](mapping, join, child) — a node in the query algebra marking a component boundary. It is NOT written by hand; the componentElaborator phase produces it from a Delegate. The interpreter, on hitting a Component, applies join to (child, cursor) and emits a deferred ProtoJson.component pointing at the target mapping. Defined in modules/core/src/main/scala/query.scala.

keyConcepts.name: componentElaborator phase
keyConcepts.explanation: A QueryCompiler.Phase auto-derived (lazily) on every Mapping from its Delegate field mappings. It walks the elaborated query and, for any Select whose (objectType, fieldName) matches a registered ComponentMapping, wraps it in Component(targetMapping, join, select). Runs after selectElaborator and before effectElaborator in Mapping.compilerPhases. Defined in modules/core/src/main/scala/compiler.scala / mapping.scala.

keyConcepts.name: Deferred execution / completeAll stitching
keyConcepts.explanation: runValue turns a Component into a ProtoJson.component(mapping, continuationQuery, cursor), an opaque deferred subtree (EffectJson with handler=None). QueryInterpreter.completeAll gathers all deferred subtrees, groups them by (mapping, handler), and for each group calls that mapping.combineAndRun(queries) in a fresh stage, recursing until no deferred subtrees remain. This is what actually runs the delegated query in the other mapping's interpreter and substitutes the results back into the enclosing JSON. Defined in modules/core/src/main/scala/queryinterpreter.scala.

keyConcepts.name: combineAndRun (batching hook)
keyConcepts.explanation: def combineAndRun(queries: List[(Query, Cursor)]): F[Result[List[ProtoJson]]] on Mapping. The default runs each (query, cursor) independently via interpreter.runOneShot. A composed component can override it to batch/group sibling delegated queries into a single backend call (the effectful CurrencyMapping in SqlComposedWorldMapping does exactly this to issue one currencies(...) lookup for many countries). Result list must stay aligned with the input list. Defined in modules/core/src/main/scala/mapping.scala.

gotchas: The composed parent needs its OWN schema, usually a superset adding the join field (e.g. Country.currency) absent from both component schemas; forgetting it leaves nowhere to hang the Delegate.
selectElaborator does NOT compose automatically: the composed mapping must re-declare cases for root fields it owns (country, fx, cities), filtering on its OWN type refs, not the component's.

The join receives the already-elaborated child query (componentElaborator runs after selectElaborator) and the parent's Cursor focused on the raw model value; you must pattern-match both and return Result.internalError on mismatch.
A join returns the OTHER mapping's field name (currency -> fx); the interpreter realigns the result name so the client still sees the original field/alias.
For a list-valued delegated field, return a Group of Selects (one per element), not a single Select returning a list; a Group where a scalar is expected (or vice versa) is a shape mismatch.
TrivialJoin (the default) only works when the field needs no parent-specific key transform - a true root field, or one the target can resolve from inherited Env/context.
ComposedCursor has focus = null and parent = None; delegated fields have no local data, so any logic reading parent.focus for a delegated subtree sees null.

Cross-mapping batching is opt-in per mapping: without overriding combineAndRun a list join is N independent backend calls. The CurrencyMapping override groups them into one (SqlComposedWorldSuite asserts count == 1). Override result lists must stay positionally aligned.
Composition is recursive (completeAll re-runs per target mapping until no deferred subtrees remain), but each level is a separate interpreter stage, so deep nesting multiplies stages.
Component is produced solely by componentElaborator from a Delegate; never construct it by hand.
